In particular, EW contributions drive the EoS toward the radiation-dominated limit earlier, reduce excursions of the speed of sound toward the causality bound, suppress transient fluctuations in the Hubble and kinematic parameters near $t \sim 10^{-5}$ s, and qualitatively change the GW spectrum from a strongly frequency-dependent signal to a flat, suppressed plateau. These results demonstrate that accurate modeling of the electroweak sector is essential for an unbiased extraction of QCD-era physics from the stochastic gravitational-wave background.
2611.22719.title: Effects of QCD Equation of State on Cosmological Parameters and Stochastic Gravitational-Waves Spectrum

2611.22723.abstract: We investigate the use of an artificial-intelligence (AI) coding agent, supervised by human physicists, for collider physics analyses using CMS Open Data. OpenAI Codex performs dimuon event selection, two-dimensional invariant-mass and decay-length fits, Monte Carlo detector simulations, and systematic uncertainty evaluation after acquiring physics and experimental knowledge from published studies and external references, with human review at each stage. The workflow is tested on two CMS datasets, with custom full-detector simulations used to determine acceptance and reconstruction efficiencies. In proton-proton collisions at sqrt(s) = 7 TeV, prompt J/psi differential cross sections are measured versus transverse momentum and rapidity. The ratios of remeasured to published CMS cross sections have a mean of 1.000 and an RMS spread of 0.215 across 39 bins. In peripheral (50-100% centrality) PbPb collisions at sqrt(s_NN) = 2.76 TeV, the corresponding prompt J/psi fiducial cross-section ratios have a mean of 1.158 and an RMS spread of 0.225 across six intervals. We identify agent failure modes and demonstrate the importance of structured human review in ensuring reliable results.
2611.22723.title: AI-Assisted Analysis of CMS Open Data: Prompt J/psi Cross-Section Measurements in pp and Peripheral PbPb Collisions at sqrt(S)= 7 TeV and sqrt(sNN) = 2.76 TeV

2611.22782.abstract: Aggregating observations into a limited number of latent tokens and learning physical interactions in the latent space has emerged as an effective approach for Transformer-based neural operators to solve Partial Differential Equation (PDE) problems involving large-scale observations. However, existing methods typically compress observations using a single aggregation pattern, making physical information not retained by that pattern invisible to the latent space and thereby constraining physical interactions within it. To address this limitation, we propose PArallel Latent Space Neural Operator (PANO), a novel neural operator for solving PDEs that formulates physical interactions among observations as an additive combination of interaction results from parallel latent spaces with shared parameters. Specifically, PANO transforms observations into multiple distinct compressed representations through independent mappings, learns physical interactions in parallel based on these representations, and finally fuses the decoded results to predict the target physical field. Within PANO, we further propose Coupled Assignment Projection (CAP) to construct bidirectionally consistent encoding and decoding mappings, and Pairwise Latent Space Attention Layer (PaLA) to jointly update latent representations of each latent space through adaptive cross-space interactions. Extensive experiments on nine benchmarks spanning diverse physical systems, geometries, and observation scales demonstrate that PANO achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, PANO reduces equivalent plastic strain prediction errors on Unilateral Stamping by 28.3% (or more) and lift-coefficient prediction errors on AirCraft by 21.4% (or more) compared with existing methods. Code is available at https://github.com/ZijiangY1116/PANO.
2611.22782.title: PANO: Parallel Latent Space Neural Operator for Solving PDEs

2611.22922.abstract: Spectral band synthesis is an important research topic in remote sensing. The Brazilian satellites CBERS-4, CBERS-4A, and AMAZONIA-1 provide high temporal resolution (1-3 days) visible and near-infrared (VNIR) imagery through the Wide-Field Imager (WFI), but lack short-wave infrared (SWIR) bands. Recent deep learning methods have shown promising results for spectral synthesis, but challenges remain for cross-satellite generalization and spectrally distant bands. This paper presents a conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) with an attention-enhanced U-net generator and a multi-loss objective to synthesize Sentinel-2/MSI SWIR bands 11 (SWIR-1) and 12 (SWIR-2) from WFI VNIR inputs. Experiments used 4,125 patches for training and cross-validation and 1,026 unseen patches for testing, with hyperparameters optimized using a subset of the training data. On SWIR-1, the model achieved SSIM of 0.900, PSNR of 31.44 dB, and MAE of 0.019 in TOA reflectance. On SWIR-2, it achieved SSIM of 0.917, PSNR of 33.35 dB, and MAE of 0.015. Benchmarking was performed on the test dataset, with each model optimized separately prior to evaluation. SWIR-cGAN outperformed the baselines, particularly for SWIR-2. The ablation study identified the multi-loss as the main performance contributor, while the attention and residual modules provided additional improvements. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of synthesizing SWIR bands from WFI imagery. The SWIR-cGAN is available at https://github.com/marujore/swir-cgan.
2611.22922.title: SWIR-cGAN: Synthesizing SWIR Bands Using VNIR Imagery from CBERS and AMAZONIA-1

2611.22951.abstract: Accurate representation of turbulent flows requires simultaneously capturing multi-scale spatial structures and the complex, nonlinear coupling between distinct physical quantities (\textit{e.g.}, velocity components and density). In practice, however, turbulent data are often constrained by low spatial resolution due to hardware limitations and computational costs. While current data-driven super-resolution methods have shown promise by learning mappings via convolutional neural networks (CNNs), they typically treat physical variables as independent channels. This simplified approach neglects intrinsic cross-variable correlations, causing models to struggle with high-fidelity reconstruction, particularly under extremely sparse conditions or in out-of-distribution regimes. To bridge this gap, we propose an architecture-agnostic spatial-physical coupling operator that extends the standard convolution into a joint spatial-variable dimension. Unlike conventional linear channel mixing, our framework constructs a unified spatial-physical representation within CNNs to explicitly capture local inter-variable interactions. By lifting features into a higher-dimensional manifold, this operator significantly enhances the model's representation capacity. Experiments demonstrate that this approach enables strong reconstruction performance and zero-shot generalization, offering a physics-aware inductive bias for super-resolution of three-dimensional turbulence. More broadly, this work suggests that high-dimensional operators offer a promising avenue for modeling intricate multi-scale turbulent flows.
2611.22951.title: A high-dimensional spatial-physical coupling operator for generalizable super-resolution of three-dimensional turbulent flows

2611.22965.abstract: Many real-world optimization problems involve optimizing black-box objectives for which only a limited number of evaluations are available. Bayesian optimization (BO) is a powerful framework for such problems, but its effectiveness often deteriorates in high-dimensional spaces. Recent work leverages diffusion models for black-box optimization, often through pre-training a reward-conditioned score network to steer generation towards high-reward samples. Alternatively, gradient-based guidance methods assume access to a differentiable reward function from which guidance gradients are queried. However, these approaches either require large amounts of labeled data for offline training or access to exact reward gradients, limiting their applicability in black-box settings. We propose BReaD (Black-box Reward-guided Sampling of Diffusion Model), a guidance sampling framework for optimizing black-box rewards without assuming access to a labeled dataset or reward gradients. The proposed method uses a Gaussian process (GP) as a differentiable surrogate for the unknown objective and actively queries labels for the generated samples. We provide a theoretical analysis of the total-variation distance between the generated distribution and the target distribution. Using Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) as guidance signals, our method balances exploration and exploitation during generation and enables the discovery of high-reward regions in the data space. Numerical experiments on scientific discovery and image generation tasks demonstrate that our framework can effectively optimize black-box rewards in low-data scenarios.
2611.22965.title: High-Dimensional Black-Box Optimization via Guidance Sampling of Diffusion Models

2611.22979.abstract: We develop greedy strategies for selecting global polynomial basis functions and training data in the sparse approximation of high-dimensional partial differential equations, with emphasis on Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equations arising in nonlinear optimal control. Inspired by the goal-oriented dual-weighted residual framework, we derive a closed-form, mesh-free indicator that predicts, to first order, the reduction of the PDE residual obtained by adding a single candidate basis function, without solving an adjoint problem. In the data-driven regime, we jointly select basis functions and gradient-augmented training samples by maximizing the predicted decrease of a supervised loss. Numerical experiments on benchmark PDEs and nonlinear optimal control problems in up to 35 dimensions show accuracy comparable to non-adaptive approaches with substantially fewer basis functions and training samples.
2611.22979.title: Residual-Driven Basis and Data Selection for Polynomial Approximation of High-Dimensional Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman Equations

2611.23069.abstract: Context. The coming decade will be the golden era of time-domain astronomy. In ten years, however, sensitive very-high-energy observations below ~1 TeV may be possible only at the two sites of the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO). Each can observe a source for only a few hours per night. Aims. We quantify the loss caused by this limited coverage and assess whether RevolIACT, an array of compact stand-alone AI-driven stations, can close the gap. Methods. We estimate the sensitivity that a stand-alone station needs to detect important transients seen by current imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes (IACTs). We also compute the temporal coverage of layouts of ten to fourteen stations distributed in longitude, and how many of the 4401 Fermi-GBM gamma-ray bursts each layout could have observed when they occurred. Results. For each station, a sensitivity of ~15 % of the Crab flux in one hour above 0.2-0.3 TeV, about three times worse than that of current IACT systems, would suffice for an array to detect most of these transients. With the standard analysis, a telescope with a 5 m diameter mirror misses this target by a factor of 17. With a video vision transformer, it comes within a factor of two in an idealised simulation, and a 6 m telescope within 1.5. Ten to fourteen stations would provide three to four times the temporal coverage of CTAO, averaged over the sky and for the GBM bursts. Fourteen stations can observe most sources around the clock for about two months per year. Conclusions. Temporal coverage, not only flux sensitivity, will limit sub-TeV transient astronomy in the next decade. RevolIACT would complement CTAO. The concept relies on the transformer analysis, which is still young and will improve. The decisive next step is to confirm this performance on real data, with a prototype station.
2611.23069.comment: 23 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Submitted for publication. Companion paper: E. Jobst et al., "A transformer analysis lowers the energy threshold and improves the sensitivity of a compact imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescope", Submitted for publication
2611.23069.title: RevolIACT: a longitudinally distributed array of compact AI-driven Cherenkov telescopes for the time-domain sub-TeV sky

2611.23135.abstract: Substantial challenges in physics-informed learning have motivated many improvements, but fragmented implementations hinder systematic organization, integration, and comparison. We propose OpenPINN/PINO, an extensible open-source PyTorch framework for physics-informed neural networks and neural operators. Two shared specifications connect problem setup, local computation, and evaluation. Agents support problem formulation, solver planning, and diagnosis. ProblemSpec defines geometry, governing equations, constitutive relations, parameters, initial and boundary conditions, and optional data. MethodSpec configures the model, sampling, loss, optimization, and differentiation. Researchers can register new problem templates and method components, then combine or compare strategies such as Fourier features, residual-adaptive sampling, and self-adaptive loss weighting for a fixed problem. Agents translate natural-language descriptions into specifications, flag missing information, and propose solver plans. The framework validates these specifications and deterministically generates local training and testing code. A diagnostic agent reviews training logs and evaluation results to identify problems and suggest revisions. Three examples show how method choices and agent diagnostics affect accuracy. For viscous Burgers, Fourier features and residual-adaptive sampling each reduced relative $L^2$ error by about $75\%$ from a shared baseline. For periodic Poisson, spectral differentiation reduced mean-free relative $L^2$ error by about $68\%$ across 16 held-out forcings. For a plate with a hole, successive agent diagnoses guided nondimensionalization and optimization. After initial training failure, all three runs met the $10\%$ target, with relative $L^2$ displacement errors of $3.51\%$--$6.31\%$.
2611.23135.comment: 53 pages. English and Chinese versions in one PDF. Code: https://github.com/junelu0214/OpenPINN-PINO
2611.23135.title: OpenPINN/PINO: An Extensible Open-Source Framework for Agent-Assisted Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Neural Operators

2611.23225.abstract: We present StringQFT as a textbook collection for string constructions of quantum field theory and as infrastructure for AI-assisted theoretical physics. The collection comprises 18 volumes, 190 chapters and 3,795 pages, covering brane probes, brane webs, geometric engineering, F-theory constructions, wrapped M5-branes and exact worldsheet constructions. Its open-book benchmark inventory contains 1,073 items, including 499 with automatic finite-answer checking. For retrieval-augmented generation, it provides 1,371 section records linked to textbook sources and PDF locations, together with a local lexical retriever. Training-data preparation is illustrated by 21 private, source-linked examples. For agents, it exposes 19 calculation tools with specified inputs and finite domains, connecting tool use to textbook derivations. We illustrate these uses through specific questions, retrieved passages and finite calculations. The textbook collection and accompanying resources are available at https://github.com/xingyang-yu/StringQFT.
2611.23225.comment: 23 pages, 6 figures. Companion paper to an 18-volume textbook collection. Textbook PDFs: https://xingyangyu.com/textbook/
2611.23225.title: StringQFT: A Multiuse Textbook Resource for AI-Assisted Theoretical Physics

2611.23226.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate frames based on new observations and inputs, making them a promising medium for interactive visual experiences. However, existing models are orders of magnitude too slow for fluid interaction. This paper introduces FastFrames, a family of fast autoregressive video diffusion models that achieves interactive latency without compromising quality. We profile the inference pipeline of state-of-the-art models and find that operations often treated as fixed implementation details, such as VAE decoding and KV cache updates, in fact account for over half of end-to-end inference latency. We challenge the assumption that these components are indispensable and replace them with lightweight alternatives. Our 1.3B variant runs at 36 ms per frame, or 28 responses per second (RPS), on a single B200 GPU while matching the generation quality of a state-of-the-art model that is nearly 8x slower. Our 14B variant runs at 45 ms per frame, or 22 RPS, on an 8x B200 GPU node and yields significantly better visual quality and realism. We show that FastFrames enables real-time interaction in applications such as camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation.
2611.23226.title: FastFrames: Video Generation at Interactive Latency

2611.23316.abstract: We present MRASLive, a toolbox for online parameter identification in time-dependent partial differential equations based on a model reference adaptive system (MRAS). Building on the MRAS proposed by Kaltenbacher and Nguyen (Inverse Problems 37(5) 2021) and its first numerical realization by the authors (Applied Mathematics for Modern Challenges 8 2026), the toolbox is designed for ease of use, utilising the user's weak form specification to prepare the data, the discretized MRAS and its solvers, and to verify the assumptions of MRAS's convergence theory semi-automatically.
2611.23316.title: MRASLive: An online parameter estimation toolbox for time-dependent PDEs

2611.23319.abstract: AI now produces machine-checked mathematics faster than researchers can read it. Can such theorems do practical computational work? We reuse one from \mbox{OpenAI's} Lean~4 relativistic Vlasov--Maxwell library: initial fields determine the field at an outside point until plasma signals reach it, and the energy leaving a surrounding box before they reach its faces. New Lean proofs and numerical bounds give particle-free references for particle-in-cell simulations across three tasks. Domain size follows analytically from observation time, exposing boundary and initialization errors in WarpX and Smilei that global energy checks missed. Grid choice can be tested directly: combining two coarse grids recovers unknown plasma inputs within tolerance at a median 14.9-fold speedup over a fine grid, where the medium grid alone fails. For reduced models, the bounds establish the minimum number of time curves needed to predict energy loss.
2611.23319.comment: 39 pages (including Supplementary Information), 8 figures, 5 ancillary files (source data and video). Submitted to Nature Computational Science
2611.23319.title: Reusing formal Vlasov-Maxwell proofs to certify plasma solver outputs

2611.23321.abstract: This review examines deep learning theory through the lens of error decomposition, systematically addressing approximation, statistical, and optimization errors. We trace the development of error analyses from bounds on individual error components to frameworks that account for all three. Using nonparametric regression and the Deep Ritz Method as dual running examples, we demonstrate how these analyses apply across fundamentally different loss structures. We then review representative analyses in scientific machine learning, generative learning, reinforcement learning, representation learning, and large language models, showing how learning errors affect solutions, distributions, and predictions through problem-specific arguments. Throughout, we clarify which error components are controlled, how they are combined, and what assumptions are needed to obtain guarantees for trained networks.
2611.23321.comment: Mathematical survey of error analysis for neural network methods, with nonparametric regression and the Deep Ritz method for elliptic PDEs as running examples. Covers function and Sobolev approximation, statistical estimation, and optimization error, together with stability estimates, convergence rates, and selected proofs
2611.23321.title: Error Analysis of Deep Learning

2611.23330.abstract: Generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are changing how researchers interact with scientific software. Their effects on productivity vary across tasks and users, but they can weaken the connection between producing a successful computational artifact and retaining scientific command over the consequential choices and evidence on which it depends. For high-energy physics, this shifts part of the training challenge from code production toward scientific stewardship: researchers must be able to validate, explain, reproduce, maintain, and justify software and workflows partly generated or modified by AI. We argue that AI-aware software training should therefore combine dedicated instruction on AI systems with the integration of AI into established software and analysis training. Testing, provenance, reproducibility, resource judgment, and scientific validation should be exercised in AI-assisted workflows, with competence judged by the evidence supporting a result rather than by code generation alone. We frame this as a problem of sustainable scientific software: AI-assisted workflows should remain trustworthy and maintainable, use computational resources responsibly, and avoid making core competence unnecessarily dependent on privileged access to particular tools or infrastructure.
2611.23330.comment: 10 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Submitted to Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence
2611.23330.title: Training for sustainable scientific software in the AI era: from code production to scientific stewardship

2611.23334.abstract: New software tools have emerged that enable AI agents to quickly develop code that analyzes data and generates figures, but their mistakes can also harm a researcher's computer, require extensive resources for validation, and cause the results to be received more skeptically. These concerns could be mitigated if scientific software is developed in a secure environment with a system for monitoring file changes and well-defined standards for handling AI agents. This paper first describes how coding agents change eleven aspects of generating, verifying, and reproducing numerical results. A six-level scale is then proposed for classifying AI-assisted numerical experiments by their provenance, reproducibility, openness, oversight, and falsifiability (PROOF). The scale begins with locally self-consistent, version-controlled, human-verified results and culminates in a publicly accessible and curated archive of the files, change history, prompt transcripts, independent agent regeneration of the analysis, and multiple cryptographically verifiable attestations of regeneration by independent researchers. These aspects of AI-assisted scientific software development have been synthesized into a new open source software package called vaibify that optimizes the agentic development of computational experiments ascending the PROOF Ladder. Docker containers sequester the agents while a GUI enables researchers to prompt command line agents, monitor the current status of local and remote files, and drive a project to PROOF Level 3 (reproducible). The methods described in this paper could help researchers reduce the time required to verify agent-written software and efficiently communicate trust in AI-assisted science.
2611.23334.comment: 36 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Software publicly available at https://github.com/RoryBarnes/vaibify
2611.23334.title: Integrating AI Coding Agents Into Scientific Research

2611.23347.abstract: Hospitals record thousands of hours of surgical video annually, yet these archives remain difficult to search by content. Surgeons cannot readily retrieve similar operations, complications, or workflow events. Existing surgical computer vision primarily produces labels rather than retrieving relevant videos. We introduce SurgCBVR, the first benchmark for content-based video-to-video retrieval in surgery. It integrates eight public datasets across four domains-ophthalmic, laparoscopic, robotic-assisted, and colonoscopy-covering six procedure types, 679 cases, and 76,489 clips (106 hours). SurgCBVR comprises two tiers: Scene, retrieving the same operative state across cases and sites, and Workflow, retrieving and localizing phase transitions and deviations. Scene includes 74,765 clips spanning 40 classes, three temporal granularities, and three playback speeds; Workflow contains 1,724 transition clips. Fixed clip lengths and frame counts, together with phase-classifier oracle and duration-only baselines, help assess label and timing shortcuts. We evaluate six generic and surgical foundation models, two video retrieval methods, and contrastive heads trained on SurgCBVR, using within-dataset, cross-dataset, and pooled-gallery retrieval restricted to the same procedure type. Frozen representations barely outperform a timing-only baseline, transition retrieval approaches chance, and trained heads lose up to half their accuracy across datasets. These findings expose substantial limitations in current video representations and establish SurgCBVR as a benchmark for advancing surgery-aware retrieval.
2611.23347.title: SurgCBVR: A Multi-Domain Benchmark for Content-Based Surgical Video-to-Video Retrieval

2611.23372.abstract: With the fourth data release (DR4) from Gaia imminent, we predict neutron star (NS) binaries with luminous companions (LCs) expected to be detectable in DR4 and the final data release (DR5). We create realistic synthetic populations of NS--LC binaries in the Milky Way using COSMIC, assuming (a) observationally motivated initial distributions of binary properties, (b) metallicity and location dependent star formation history of the MW adopted from the FIRE-2 galaxy m12i, and (c) all relevant binary interaction physics, with the rapid and delayed supernova prescriptions. We estimate the detectable NS--LC population using an approximate Gaia\ selection function based on projected orbital size of the LC as well as gaiamock, which emulates Gaia's multi-epoch astrometry and orbit-fitting pipeline- both after taking into account extinction and reddening. Across supernova models and statistical fluctuations, the former (gaiamock) pipeline predicts $\sim14$--$29$ ($\sim1$--$8$), $4500$--$4700$ ($100$--$110$), and $4800$--$5000$ ($300$--$380$) detectable NS--LC binaries in DR3, DR4, and DR5, respectively. While the orbital-size based pipeline brackets the DR3 yield of NS--LC candidates, the gaiamock prediction falls short, suggesting uncertainties in the modeled binary evolution or contributions from other formation channels. DR4 is expected to directly shed light on the the relative importance of detectable NS--LC binaries from isolated binary evolution vis a vis other channels such as dynamical formation. Interestingly, our models suggest that future releases will also include $22^{+7}_{-5}\ (13^{+5}_{-4})$ and $124^{+14}_{-15}\ (53^{+10}_{-6})$ gaiamock-detectable pulsar--MS binaries in DR4 and DR5, respectively, for the rapid (delayed) model, which are prime targets for radio follow-up.
2611.23372.comment: 28 pages, 13 figures, 1 table, submitted to the Astrophysical Journal; comments welcome
2611.23372.title: Gaia's promise to detect compact-object binaries II: Predictions for dormant neutron star binaries in DR4 and beyond

2611.23389.abstract: Diffuse gamma rays above 100 TeV probe PeV cosmic rays and astrophysical neutrino sources. Their strong attenuation on background radiation makes the observed flux sensitive to the location of the emission and to possible modifications of photon propagation. Searches for an isotropic component require rejection of an overwhelming hadronic background, but uncertainties in air-shower physics, cosmic-ray composition and detector response can lead to differences between simulated and measured events. Here we report upper limits on the isotropic diffuse gamma-ray flux from 100 TeV to 10 PeV using 1078 days of Carpet-3 observations collected between 2022 and 2026. We identify photon candidates with a neural network combining the surface-array signals and measurements from the upgraded 410 $\mathrm{m^2}$ muon detector. Unsupervised domain adaptation uses unlabeled experimental events during training to mitigate the impact of simulation--data discrepancies on the classification. The limits are among the strongest available and provide benchmarks for tests of extended Galactic emission and modified photon propagation from extragalactic sources.
2611.23389.title: Isotropic diffuse gamma-ray flux limits from Carpet-3 experiment data using neural networks with domain adaptation

2611.23440.abstract: Selecting less computation in a neural operator need not reduce inference time. We study this gap using conformal calibration to choose Fourier modes or channel width per input subject to a fixed error budget. A triangle-inequality envelope bounds all candidates simultaneously; a direct-score rule handles non-monotone candidate errors and, with an input-independent score, calibrates a static baseline under the same marginal guarantee. Under frozen-model and exchangeability assumptions, both rules bound the probability of issuing a prediction outside the budget and abstain when calibration is infeasible. On Burgers and Darcy flow across three training seeds, mode selection reduces active spectral support without a measurable latency reduction, because full-grid transforms and channel mixing dominate the cost. Narrowing channels does reduce Darcy forward cost, but reference-based selection must first compute the dense prediction. An input-only binary width selector avoids that pass and runs at 0.52-0.95 times dense latency; yet static widths calibrated under the same rule are often as fast or faster, and on a separately generated 1,000-example test set they generally achieve higher coverage, while the selector falls below its 90% target in more than half of the settings. Adaptive computation in neural operators should therefore be judged by achieved coverage and complete runtime against a matched static comparator.
2611.23440.title: Conformally Calibrated Adaptive Computation in Neural Operators

2611.23467.abstract: Transport maps provide a powerful framework for the generative modeling of complex, non-Gaussian spatial fields, such as those encountered in climate science. By mapping a complicated target distribution to a standard Gaussian reference distribution, they can serve as efficient stochastic surrogates. However, current Bayesian transport maps, which are modeled using autoregressive Gaussian processes, typically rely on empirical Bayes estimates that ignore hyperparameter uncertainty. Here, we contrast this point-estimate approach with a fully Bayesian model that provides posterior uncertainty quantification in transport map hyperparameters. To avoid the high cost of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), we also propose a Laplace approximation to the hyperparameter posteriors, which can be computed at negligible additional computational cost relative to empirical Bayes. We provide numerical evidence and a real-data climate application demonstrating that these Laplace approximations can accurately capture most posterior summaries at a fraction of the cost of MCMC, while maintaining good predictive properties. Thus, our approach offers a scalable, uncertainty-aware framework for the generative modeling of non-Gaussian climate fields.
2611.23467.title: Laplace Bayesian transport maps for generative modeling of non-Gaussian climate fields

2611.23486.abstract: In this paper, we argue that the brain is a complex dynamical system in a critical state similar to that of the 3D Ising model. We highlight several properties of the brain, including resonance phenomena within this critical state, long-range autocorrelations consistent with long memory, a hysteresis zone suggesting the presence of an as yet undetected "exotic" type of matter within the brain, and possible quantum phenomena within the microtubules of neural networks. The latter suggests that these structures exhibit a combined form of "logical superposition". In the proposed model, "AND" logic would require two distinct quantum states to be occupied simultaneously. The proposed "OR" logic allows any one of several quantum states to be occupied at a time. Moreover, we propose that kink and antikink solitons could mediate coupling between occupied quantum states in the microtubules and thereby contribute to pattern formation in neural networks. This mechanism may well be what gives the brain the flexibility to support complex thought and other cognitive functions.
2611.23486.comment: 38 pages, 11 numbered figures and 1 unnumbered illustration
2611.23486.title: How the material world of the brain, as a complex system governed by intermittent dynamics, gives rise to the supposedly "immaterial" world of mental processes such as thought

2611.23492.abstract: Spectra from different surveys carry different systematics and are not calibrated against one another. Multi-survey foundation models for stellar spectra are then built by aligning embeddings of the same star observed across surveys. Most in astronomy follow the recipes established for language and vision, aligning with a contrastive loss that separates every star from the others. However, this does not ensure that the stellar physics is encoded in a form that a simple read-out can recover. Holding the cross-survey architecture fixed and varying only the alignment loss, we measure what an objective encodes from the principal-component geometry of the Gaia BP/RP (XP) spectra and from a linear probe of the stellar parameters. In a properly aligned embedding, the leading two principal components form a plane that recovers an analog of the Kiel diagram, the third component tracks [Fe/H], and [alpha/Fe] varies coherently across the plane, such that the chemically defined Galactic disks and accreted populations occupy distinct loci. We show that legibility, the ease of reading the information out, is highest for a training objective that never pushes stars apart, and instead constrains only the overall distribution of each survey's embeddings (JEPA). JEPA also exceeds the contrastive alternative at the same architecture, and the performance improves further as more surveys (Gaia XP+LAMOST LRS+DESI+APOGEE) are included. Predicted abundances for 8.0 million XP giants reproduce the main [alpha/Fe]-[Fe/H] structure of the Milky Way. These results indicate that the choice of alignment objective, not alignment alone, determines whether stellar labels are linearly recoverable.
2611.23492.comment: 15 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to AAS journals. Comments welcome
2611.23492.title: JEPA for astronomy: multi-survey spectral alignment puts stellar parameters on the leading principal axes

2611.23526.abstract: Parameter estimation in chaotic models often relies on prescribed summary statistics, whose ability to constrain parameters may be difficult to establish in advance. Different parameters influence different features and time scales of the dynamics, so the record length and sampling interval needed to constrain them may differ. We choose to learn a representation directly from the trajectory and use it as our summary statistic. The recurrent encoder that produces this representation is trained jointly with a conditional normalizing flow for amortized posterior estimation. We use the Lorenz-63 and two-scale Lorenz-96 systems to investigate how inference depends on the observed variables, record length and sampling interval, and compare our results with the state-of-the-art Calibrate--Emulate--Sample method. In Lorenz-96, learned summaries of a 2 model-time-unit (MTU) record achieve estimation skill comparable to prescribed second-moment statistics from substantially longer records for several parameters. Fast-process parameters remain weakly constrained by slow-variable records across the tested 2 to 100 MTU windows, while adding fast-field averages improves their recovery from 2 MTU. Coarser sampling weakens inference from fast-field observations, but longer coverage can partly compensate. Once trained for a given observation setting, the estimator we develop returns posteriors for compatible records without further model integration. These proof-of-concept results illustrate how data-driven learning of summaries can be used to inform the design of observations in dynamical systems.
2611.23526.title: Linking Dynamical Time Scales and Experimental Design to Parameter Identifiability from Time-Series Observations

2611.23539.abstract: We present a framework for constructing deployable hard-constrained turbulence closures of unclosed terms in the transport equations of Reynolds stresses and turbulent dissipation rate. The framework is built from modules, each performing a single task. The closure module represents the closure with a small network, while the state module represents the flow state during training. The closure network is coupled to the state network through the governing equation residuals, allowing the closure to be learned without reference closure values being supplied as training data. The coordinate module learns monotone input coordinates that help both networks resolve sharp changes. Within the network architecture, the boundary condition (BC) module imposes boundary values exactly using the Theory of Functional Connections, and the realizability module keeps the closure realizable. We apply the framework to decaying homogeneous isotropic turbulence (HIT) with experimental and direct numerical simulation trajectories. Here, the state module is a Deep Operator Network (DeepONet), the BC module imposes the initial state and the closure's low and high Reynolds number limits, and the realizability module ensures growth of the Taylor microscale. Across ten random seeds, the framework reduces root-mean-square seed-to-seed closure variation by about 95\% relative to the unconstrained model over the training and held-out range. The deployed 18-parameter closure network requires only the Taylor scale Reynolds number and can be exported as a standalone C function.
2611.23539.title: Construction of a Deployable Hard-Constrained Turbulence Closure

2611.23561.abstract: Earthquake sequence simulations involve slow interseismic processes and rapid dynamic ruptures. During interseismic periods, a numerical solver can take large time steps efficiently. During seismic periods, in contrast, the solver must drastically reduce the time step, and elastodynamic wave-mediated memory effects become significant; long-term simulations are therefore computationally expensive. We investigate the use of neural operators to accelerate earthquake sequence simulations. We train a Fourier neural operator (FNO) on data from high-fidelity, fully dynamic simulations to learn a jump map that advances the system state from before a seismic rupture to after it. We propose a hybrid modeling framework in which a conventional quasi-dynamic solver simulates the slow interseismic evolution, and the trained FNO replaces the solver during the computationally intensive seismic periods with wave-mediated inertial effects. The hybrid model reproduces key long-term statistics of fully dynamic simulations, including distributions of event magnitudes and recurrence times. Furthermore, it provides a much better approximation to the fully dynamic simulations than the commonly used quasi-dynamic approximation at a reduced computational expense.
2611.23561.title: Machine-learned acceleration of earthquake sequence simulations

2611.23563.abstract: Many learning-based approaches for deformable linear objects (DLOs) rely on simplified deformation models that neglect dynamic effects and the mechanical response of the objects, limiting their applicability to lightweight, compliant objects and slow motions. Inspired by recent advances in learning physically structured dynamics with coupled oscillator networks (CONs), we propose $Φ$-CON for learning force-driven DLO dynamics. The model combines a floating-base coupled oscillator network (FBCON), whose latent potential energy depends only on the DLO's shape, with a learned affine diffeomorphism $Φ$ between observed positions along the DLO and latent coordinates. Its shape dynamics are stable by construction, and its Lagrangian structure yields explicit expressions for kinetic and potential energy. We exploit this structure to design a model-based proportional-derivative (PD) controller that compensates for the learned potential forces, thereby establishing closed-loop stability guarantees and ensuring convergence. We evaluate the approach on four simulated DLOs and a real bimanual robot setup. In simulation, $Φ$-CON achieves prediction accuracy comparable to neural ordinary differential equation (NODE) models and Lagrangian neural networks (LNNs), with $97.2\%$ and $90.2\%$ fewer parameters, respectively. Relative to a model-free PD baseline, the proposed controller reduces mean endpoint regulation error by $97.5$-$99.7\%$ in simulation and achieves a mean per-target reduction of $27.9\%$ across both endpoints in real-world experiments, demonstrating the importance of explicitly accounting for the mechanical response of stiff and heavy objects.
2611.23563.title: Learning the Dynamics of Deformable Linear Objects Through Coupled Oscillators for Bimanual Robotic Manipulation

2611.23639.abstract: In cosmology, surveys span different sky regions and wavelength ranges, resulting in uneven modality coverage across observational datasets. Such heterogeneity can be addressed through either multimodal foundation models (FMs), which learn shared embedding spaces, or independently learned modality embeddings combined via late fusion. We investigate whether the latter provides an adaptive alternative to FM-based scientific retrieval. We evaluate this approach on a galaxy retrieval task spanning diverse modalities--history of star formation, spectra of light emitted, and multi-wavelength observations from two telescopes--comparing an FM baseline with separately trained embeddings fused through multi-objective optimization based on Pareto optimality. We find that the FM baseline achieves strong embedding-space proximity, but our method preserves modality-specific distance structure that allows scientists to inspect which physical signals drive similarity. Our method also achieves improved fidelity in raw-data space: across six measured properties, its nearest neighbor is 8% closer to the query on average than that retrieved by kNN in the FM embedding space (spread 0.128 vs. 0.139). These results suggest that multi-objective retrieval can surface astrophysically coherent candidates that single-objective search alone may overlook.
2611.23639.title: Searching the Pareto Front: Multi-Objective Retrieval for Heterogeneous Scientific Modalities

2611.23760.abstract: Determining unique atomic coordinates from powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) remains challenging because peak overlap, weak scattering from light elements, limited scattering contrast between elements with similar atomic numbers, and experimental noise render the inverse problem underdetermined. Here, we present XCAPE (XRD-Constrained Accelerated Prediction Engine), a crystal structure prediction (CSP) framework that integrates experimentally derived composition, unit cell parameters, space group, and PXRD data into a symmetry-aware evolutionary search. XCAPE explores Wyckoff-site configurations using tailored mutation operations, evaluates candidates by both energetic stability and diffraction agreement, and accelerates geometry optimization using a universal machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP). The framework recovered 71 of 77 database-derived benchmark structures (92.2%) from simulated PXRD patterns and all 12 reference structures from experimental PXRD patterns. It further identified 12 candidate structure assignments that are consistent with experimental PXRD patterns, lack matching entries in the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database (ICSD), and are thermodynamically competitive at the MLIP level. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations showed that 10 of these 12 candidates lie within 10 meV/atom of the convex hull. By bridging experimental diffraction data and physically plausible atomistic models, XCAPE can provide structural insight into previously unresolved materials and support accelerated materials discovery in automated research workflows.
2611.23760.comment: 15 pages, 7 figures. Supporting Information is available as an ancillary file
2611.23760.title: Physics-Guided Crystal Structure Elucidation from Powder X-Ray Diffraction with Universal Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials

2611.23773.abstract: The search for a low-dimensional subspace that governs neural network training has been a persistent goal in optimization. Yet subspaces defined by Hessian eigenvalue magnitude, such as the dominant/bulk decomposition underlying Dom-SGD and Bulk-SGD, have repeatedly failed to capture where optimization takes place, and adaptive Krylov-based alternatives built on energy-fraction thresholds show promise but still struggle at lower eigenmodes. We argue this failure is structural: the directions of highest curvature are not, in general, the directions along which training moves. We introduce the dominant aligned subspace (DAS), constructed from a full eigendecomposition of the Hessian but selected by gradient alignment rather than eigenvalue magnitude, as a tool for understanding optimization dynamics and a foundation for designing methods that exploit them. To expose this structure under the hardest conditions, we use physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) as a testbed: differential operators from the parabolic, elliptic, and hyperbolic classes induce severely ill-conditioned, anisotropic loss landscapes. Across Poisson, heat, wave, and viscous Burgers benchmarks DAS-restricted training with a line search matches full-space training even where the projected Hessian remains ill-conditioned, showing empirically that convergence does not require all Hessian eigendirections but only a low-dimensional, gradient-aligned subset. We extend the analysis to Gauss-Newton within the DAS and discuss what this structure implies for future subspace-aware optimizers.
2611.23773.comment: 57 pages, 17 figures, 7 tables. In the title, n-DAS denotes an optimizer of order n restricted to the dominant aligned subspace (DAS): 1-DAS for first-order and 2-DAS for second-order methods
2611.23773.title: A Systematic Analysis of a Small Optimal Subspace for Physics-Informed Neural Networks: $n$-DAS $\subset \mathbb{R}^p$

2611.23776.abstract: Accelerator-based muon imaging combines the penetrating power of high-energy muons with selectable momentum and a controlled beam direction, offering a powerful means of probing internal structures in large, dense and heavily shielded objects. Within a fixed beam-time budget, realizing this potential requires reliable recovery of fine structures from limited muon statistics. We propose an observation-conditioned residual diffusion method with decoupled linear schedules to enhance low-count muon images through iterative restoration guided by the observed image. We evaluate a simplified VSC-24 fuel cask under an idealized 5 GeV parallel muon beam, using 500,000 accepted events per low-count image and 40 million per reference image. Simulation results show improved recovery of structural boundaries and fine details, with the mean peak signal-to-noise ratio increasing from 11.4239 to 22.1719 dB. These findings highlight the potential of diffusion models to make more effective use of limited muon data and broaden the application of accelerator-based muon imaging across scientific and industrial settings.
2611.23776.title: Residual diffusion for fine-structure enhancement in low-count accelerator-based muon imaging

2611.23801.abstract: In this paper we study active learning for constrained linear regression. Given a design matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, a constraint set $C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$, and query access to $b\in\mathbb{R}^n$, we seek an approximate solution to $\min_{x\in C}\|Ax-b\|_2^2$ using as few queries as possible. This problem arises in many scientific and engineering applications, and randomized leverage score sampling provides a powerful method to solve it. However, existing leverage score methods ignore the constraint or encode it through ridge regularization, suffering unfavorable query complexity for anisotropic constraint sets. We propose ellipsoid-regularized leverage scores, where we approximate the constraint set by an outer ellipsoid and use its shape matrix to bias sampling toward directions that matter under the constraint geometry. We prove that the query complexity is governed by an anisotropic effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}}(C)\le d$. With appropriate parameters, $O(d_{\text{eff}}(C)\log d/\varepsilon^2)$ queries suffice to return a point in $C$ with objective value at most $(1+\varepsilon)$ times the optimum. This bound can substantially improve on the standard leverage-score bound, since anisotropic constraints can make $d_{\text{eff}}(C)$ much smaller than $d$. For convex constraints, we improve the dependence on $\varepsilon$ from $1/\varepsilon^2$ to $1/\varepsilon$. We also prove two lower bounds: first, the $d/\varepsilon^2$ dependence is unavoidable without convexity assumptions on $C$, and second, in some regimes, the effective dimension dependence $d_{\mathrm{eff}}(C)/\varepsilon$ is necessary for ellipsoidal constraints. Experiments on synthetic regression problems and a parametric heat conduction problem show lower regression error than standard baselines for similar query budget.
2611.23801.title: Improved Leverage Score Sampling for Constrained Active Linear Regression

2611.23818.abstract: The James Webb Space Telescope is delivering unprecedented constraints on exoplanet atmospheres, but computationally intensive Bayesian retrievals challenge the transition from individual planets to population-level studies of planetary formation and evolution. We introduce NEXONN, a transformer-conditioned normalizing-flow framework within NEXOTRANS that enables rapid atmospheric posterior estimation with uncertainty quantification. Incorporating PandExo-based JWST noise, we benchmark NEXONN against PyMultiNest using simulated spectra and JWST observations of WASP-39 b (0.6-12 microns). For simulated MIRI/LRS data, eight posteriors achieve a mean overlap of 80.32%. Retrievals of combined NIRISS, NIRSpec, and MIRI observations yield consistent atmospheric properties. For the full dataset, NEXONN infers C/O = 0.82 (+0.01/-0.02) and [M/H] = 1.13 (+0.04/-0.04), compared with PyMultiNest values of 0.80 (+0.03/-0.01) and 1.19 (+0.05/-0.03). Divergence metrics, Wasserstein distances, posterior overlaps, and coverage tests assess posterior fidelity and uncertainty calibration, revealing parameter-dependent differences. Once trained, NEXONN performs posterior inference within seconds, enabling scalable population studies of exoplanet atmospheric composition, formation, and evolution.
2611.23818.comment: 28 pages, 11 figures, 3 tables. Revised and resubmitted to The Astronomical Journal. We thank the anonymous referee for their constructive comments. Further comments are welcome
2611.23818.title: NEXONN: Advancing the NEXOTRANS Exoplanet Atmospheric Retrieval Framework with Transformer-Based Neural Posterior Estimation for JWST Transmission Spectroscopy of WASP-39b

2611.23834.abstract: We study the unpolarized generalized parton distributions (GPDs) of the nucleon in a covariant quark-diquark approach, in which both scalar and axial-vector diquarks are treated as composite subsystems. Motivated by previous form factor studies, we introduce a vertex correction based on the pion cloud picture as a first exploratory treatment of pion cloud effects at the GPD level, in order to improve the description of $E^q(ξ, x, t)$ and related magnetic observables. At the model input scale, only valence quarks are included. With the vertex correction, the electromagnetic form factors $G_{E, M}$ and the mass form factor $A$ obtained from the Mellin moments of the GPDs agree well with those obtained from direct calculations. The vertex correction brings the evolved charge weighted distribution $\sum{e^q E^q(ξ, x, t)}$ closer to the phenomenological parametrization. The correction shifts transverse strength from the central region toward the peripheral region, consistent with the long range character of the pion cloud contribution. The transverse structure results further suggest a harder longitudinal momentum distribution in the central region of the nucleon than in its periphery. Furthermore, the evolved real part of the proton Compton form factor, $\mathrm{Re} \mathcal{H}(ξ, t)$, has a reasonable magnitude and follows the main trend of the Quantum Deep Neural Networks (QDNN) extraction. In addition, $\mathrm{Re} \mathcal{H}$ may be more sensitive to the ERBL region than the other physical quantities calculated in this work.
2611.23834.title: Unpolarized Generalized Parton Distributions of the Nucleon in a Covariant Quark-Diquark Approach

2611.23837.abstract: Materials discovery often requires chemical extrapolation beyond labeled data. When target compounds contain elements absent from training, which compounds of other elements provide transferable supervision remains unclear. Here we show that, without target-property labels, materials representations rank other elements by the supervision their compounds provide. Engineered descriptors rank them largely by elemental-property similarity, whereas a pretrained crystal-graph encoder ranks them by the geometry of its learned representation. At fixed training-set size, excluding the compounds of the encoder's six top-ranked elements raises formation-energy and bandgap errors by 100-110 meV per atom and 42-85 meV, versus little change for six lower-ranked elements. The rankings hold across properties, regressors and datasets. The encoder's ranking outperforms elemental-property similarity and periodic groups, suggesting that it captures how elements behave within compounds. Materials representations thus organize transferable supervision, which can be identified before model training, informing dataset assessment and label acquisition.
2611.23837.title: Materials representations organize transferable supervision for chemical extrapolation

2611.23863.abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting models, chiefly trained on reanalysis data, now match or beat physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) models on most headline scores, but whether this advantage extends to extreme weather is contested. We review peer-reviewed studies that directly compare data-driven forecasts with NWP for extremes, from nowcasting to subseasonal lead times. We discuss grey literature in the outlook but do not include it in the formal review. There is good agreement on the fact that data-driven models mostly outperform NWP on temperature extremes, tropical cyclone tracks and the location of synoptic features across time scales. The evidence is mixed for extreme precipitation and feature-based extreme event detection such as extremes related to atmospheric rivers, while it leans toward better NWP performance for estimating event intensity. For record-breaking events that lie outside the training distribution, the evidence is narrower. Nonetheless, both a systematic global evaluation and several case studies find that physics-based models retain the advantage, with data-driven models underestimating both the frequency and the magnitude of records. Hybrid systems that post-process NWP with machine-learning (ML), or couple data-driven forecasts with physics-based models, deliver some of the largest and most consistent gains. We argue that headline scores, verification choices and case selection explain much of the apparent disagreement in the literature, and provide recommendations for a more trustworthy and interpretable evaluation of data-driven models for extreme and record-breaking weather.
2611.23863.title: Comparing Data-Driven and Numerical Weather Prediction Forecasts of Extreme Weather: A Review

2611.23873.abstract: Universal machine learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) make atomistic simulations possible at scales beyond the reach of density functional theory (DFT). Matlantis PFP is a uMLIP that treats a variety of domains, including crystals, molecules, and surfaces, with a single model. PFP v8 incorporated a training dataset computed with the r2SCAN functional, chosen for its good agreement with experiment, but the elements and domains covered by that dataset were limited. Here we present Matlantis PFP v9, in which the training data computed with the r2SCAN functional are extended to the lanthanides from Pr to Lu and to the elements from Po to Cm, for a total of 96 elements, and to additional domains such as clusters and adsorption structures. The formation energies of crystals containing the newly supported elements reproduce experimental standard enthalpies of formation with the same level of accuracy as crystals composed only of previously supported elements, and the adsorption energies of molecules on transition-metal surfaces have an overall error against experiment comparable to that of DFT-PBE, although chemisorbed species are overbound. On the same type of GPU (A100), the inference speed and the maximum system size exceed those of SevenNet-Omni, a public uMLIP trained on r2SCAN data: forces are evaluated three to four times faster, and five to ten times as many atoms can be handled. As a result, PFP-R2SCAN is now applicable to systems containing rare-earth and actinide elements and to adsorption on surfaces.
2611.23873.title: Technical Note on Matlantis PFP v9: Extending the Element and Domain Coverage of the r2SCAN Training Data

2611.23906.abstract: A phantom-divide transition favored by recent cosmological observations poses an inverse problem: which field potentials realize the inferred expansion history, and what features are uniquely fixed by it? We reconstruct local potentials for a canonical-phantom scalar pair with standard matter and radiation, targeting Metastable Emergent Dark Energy histories constrained by CMB, DESI BAO, and Type Ia supernova data. The coupled-field Friedmann evolution reproduces the target background to numerical accuracy across the transition, with regular perturbations through the crossing. At the phantom divide, the transition slope sets a dimensionless potential-energy release rate insensitive to the partition of kinetic energy. We identify local potential deformations that preserve both background expansion and linear dynamics. This construction gives a classical field realization of the inferred transition and disentangles observationally fixed energy balances from interaction terms requiring additional theoretical input.
2611.23906.title: Inverse Reconstruction of Two-Field Potentials for a DESI-Motivated Phantom-Divide Transition

2611.23909.abstract: Radio Access Network (RAN) slicing is a shared resource allocation problem: each slice seeks to satisfy its Service Level Agreement (SLA) with minimal radio-resource consumption, while all slices compete for a limited resource budget. This creates both an intra-slice trade-off between SLA assurance and resource efficiency and an inter-slice conflict over shared resources, calling for specialized yet coordinated control. In this work, we present CoSlice, a coordinated multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for inter-slice physical resource block allocation in Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN). CoSlice uses preference-conditioned slice agents for fast resource allocation and an LLM-based coordinator to adapt their objectives using global network observations at a slower timescale. We formulate the problem as a multi-objective partially observable stochastic game (mo-POSG), establish the existence of a Preference Correlated Equilibrium, and derive a sublinear regret bound for the learning procedure. We implement the algorithm by using a two-stage training procedure that consists of multi-objective pretraining and joint optimization. We build a network slicing evaluation environment using ORANSlice and its radio-frequency simulator (RFsim), supporting realistic protocol-stack execution and application traffic across multiple slices. Experimental results show that CoSlice reduces both average and tail SLA violations compared with other centralized and multi-agent baselines under diverse slice workloads.
2611.23909.title: CoSlice: Coordinated Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for 5G Network Slicing Allocation

2611.24013.abstract: Scaling universal quantum computation and implementing quantum machine learning with protected logical qubits remain challenging. To harness the computational potential of existing fault-tolerant quantum platforms, we introduce topological quantum reservoir computing, a novel approach using protected degrees of freedom for storage and the host system's intrinsic dynamics for information processing. Using a one-dimensional Kitaev chain, we show how long-lived Majorana edge modes and fast bulk responses support these complementary functions within the same many-body system. We identify the tradeoffs governing access to protected memory and show how matched interfaces enable programmable writing and interactions enable autonomous information consolidation from the bulk to the edge. These mechanisms improve performance on tasks requiring long-term retention of temporal information. Our results establish topology as a new resource for quantum reservoir computing and open a route toward near-term quantum computing and quantum machine learning.
2611.24013.title: Topological Quantum Reservoir Computing

2611.24020.abstract: The hydroxyl radical (OH) is the main oxidant in the troposphere and accounts for 88% of the methane sink, yet its abundance and trends remain poorly constrained. Satellites observe many of the chemical and meteorological drivers of OH, but assimilating both requires a model that represents chemistry and meteorology together. Existing chemistry-climate models are too expensive for joint data assimilation. Here, we present AuroraChem, a fine-tuned version of the Aurora atmospheric foundation model that jointly simulates meteorology and the GEOS-Chem chemical fields needed to constrain OH. A one-year AuroraChem rollout takes 12 minutes on one GPU. Free rollouts remain stable for one year but do not fully capture seasonal cycles. Using idealized data assimilation, we find that chemical observations can constrain the meteorological state and meteorological observations can constrain the chemical state. Inserting only the chemical fields raises the annual mean spatial correlation of 500 hPa temperature from 0.89 to 0.92 and recovers the moisture and circulation pattern of the Indian summer monsoon. Inserting only the meteorological fields raises the 500 hPa OH correlation from 0.89 to 0.93, close to the 0.94 from inserting the chemical fields themselves, and recovers the OH seasonal cycle. Inserting only NO2 columns sampled at TROPOMI pixels gives an OH correlation of 0.93. These relationships likely reflect learned covariances rather than physical coupling, and covariances are what data assimilation uses to let an observation of one variable update the others. AuroraChem therefore provides a new pathway to joint chemical and meteorological data assimilation.
2611.24020.title: Enabling joint chemical and meteorological data assimilation with an atmospheric foundation model

2611.24088.abstract: Modern equivariant machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have dramatically improved the accuracy of and the scales accessible to atomistic simulation, yet the thermodynamic sampling methods needed to turn those potentials into finite-temperature phase stability predictions have not kept pace computationally. We present the GPU-native, massively parallel nested sampling framework JAXRENS, implemented on top of JAX, which removes the practical bottlenecks preventing atomistic nested sampling from being combined with state-of-the-art MLIPs. The framework provides distributed multi-GPU execution, vectorised ensembles of walkers, and direct interoperability with modern force fields. We demonstrate the highly beneficial scaling of JAXRENS on hardware accelerators, and apply it to the simulation of the ZnS phase diagram based on a MACE foundation model, a procedure previously computationally inaccessible. Despite requiring in the order of 10^10 model evaluations, the final converged simulation completed within six days on four GPUs, marking an important step towards routine, first-principles-quality predictions of finite-temperature phase stability using machine-learned interatomic potentials.
2611.24088.title: A GPU-Native Nested Sampling Framework for Finite-Temperature Materials Modelling with Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials

2611.24089.abstract: Quantum annealing is a promising quantum algorithm for dealing with computationally hard optimization problems. Currently available hardware can implement the algorithm for a significant class of Hamiltonian problems. However, its performance is especially limited in discontinuous quantum phase transitions, where the energy gap shrinks exponentially with system size. In this paper, we introduce an extension of quantum annealing to a quantum neural network and study its performance in a number of prototypical optimization problems. In particular, we observe that already a random quantum annealing network of width W = 2 can exponentially reduce the number of evolution layers or depth of the annealing process in the quantum search problem. By tuning the network parameters the search problem can be solved with exponentially small errors by a quantum perceptron of depth L = 1 and width W = 2. The findings show that width of a quantum annealing network is critical to enhance the success probability of the algorithm by providing a larger and learnable evolution space for the annealing process.
2611.24089.title: Quantum Annealing with a Quantum Neural Network: Width of Annealing Matters

2611.24091.abstract: Rare processes at the Large Hadron Collider often lead to final states with quarks, for which the dominant backgrounds contain the same reconstructed objects as the signal. The colour structure of the hard process, imprinted on the pattern of soft QCD radiation, carries information that is largely left unused by standard analyses. We introduce a geometric representation of this colour flow by mapping hadronic constituents onto the unit sphere through a modified inverse stereographic projection centred on a pair of jets selected as a colour-singlet resonance candidate. The jet separation defines a circular region whose interior and exterior are mapped to opposite hemispheres, allowing a graph neural network to exploit the resulting radiation pattern using geodesic distances. As a benchmark, we consider flavour-changing neutral interactions of the top quark with the Higgs boson at $\sqrt{s}=13.6$~TeV, through associated $tH$ production and $t\bar t$ production with one top quark undergoing a $t\to qH$ decay, where $q=u,c$, focusing on subsequent $H\to b\bar b$ and leptonically top quark decays in both channels. Relative to a baseline graph neural network operating in the $(η,φ)$ plane, the geodesic-aware network improves the expected 95\% confidence-level limits on $\mathrm{BR}(t\to uH)$ and $\mathrm{BR}(t\to cH)$ by about an order of magnitude, to $1.1\times10^{-4}$ and $8.3\times10^{-5}$ for an assumed integrated luminosity of $139~\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$. The approach can also be applied to searches for other colour-singlet resonances decaying into quarks or gluons.
2611.24091.comment: 42 pages including references; 12 figures and 8 tables
2611.24091.title: Improving Sensitivity to Rare Processes at the LHC with Geodesic-Aware Graph Neural Networks

2611.24130.abstract: The quantum position operator and its response to perturbations underpin the functional properties of insulating materials. In the modern theory of polarization, Wannier charge centres encode Berry-phase polarization, while their structural derivatives determine key response functions. Here we introduce a universal diffusion model based on E(3)-equivariant graph neural networks for moments of the position operator, with the first moment defining Wannier centres and the second central moment their real-space localization. We demonstrate the framework for liquid water, amorphous silicon and crystalline BaTiO$_3$, and train a universal model that generalizes to 100 unseen crystals spanning a 67-species chemical space. The predicted centres reproduce infrared spectra in large liquid and amorphous cells beyond routine first-principles reach and enable finite-difference calculations of Born effective charges and piezoelectric tensors. This framework provides a scalable route to electronic polarization and localization in complex materials, supporting high-throughput screening and finite-temperature simulations.
2611.24130.title: A Universal Diffusion Model for the Quantum Position Operator

2611.24148.abstract: Photopolymerization of acrylated epoxidized soybean oil (AESO) is a convenient model of a self-organizing process in a soft, bio-based material: ultraviolet light starts a free-radical chain reaction, the growing network releases heat, and the mobility of molecular groups changes on several time scales at once. We follow this process from two sides. Experimentally, the real and imaginary parts of the dielectric permittivity of an AESO:VDM (1:0.5) mixture with 3 mol% of the photoinitiator DMPA were recorded at 500-5000 Hz under an intermittent on/off illumination protocol, and the resulting time series were analysed with a sliding-window Shannon entropy and the Grassberger-Procaccia correlation integral. Both measures show that short light pulses at the start of curing trigger strongly correlated, collective relaxation, which fades as the network forms, leaving only localized reorientations active. We describe these reorientations as orientational defects and quantify their energetics with the MACE-OFF23 machine learning interatomic potential, using relaxed dihedral scans of five rotational modes ($α$, $α/β$, $β$, $γ$, $δ$) of an AESO fragment. Compared with density functional theory (DFT) reference profiles, MACE reproduces the shape of all five profiles (Pearson $r=0.95$-$0.98$) and the hierarchy of barriers - from 2.9 eV for the constrained main-chain rotation, through 0.54-0.81 eV for the acrylate rotations, to 0.16-0.18 eV for the methyl and 0.06 eV for the hydroxyl rotation - while underestimating the barrier heights by 3-20%. A simple Arrhenius estimate shows that the acrylate rotations are the modes closest to the frequency window of the dielectric measurement.
2611.24148.comment: 15 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Preprint of a chapter published in the NATO Science for Peace and Security Series B: Physics and Biophysics (Springer, 2025)
2611.24148.title: Machine learning interatomic potentials and orientational defects in polymers

2611.24261.abstract: Cosmic-ray particles in the TeV range, originating outside the solar system, are partially blocked on their way to Earth by the Moon, producing a deficit in their flux known as the Moon shadow. This work presents a precision measurement of the westward shift of the Moon's shadow using 3.4 years of data from LHAASO's Water Cherenkov Detector Array (WCDA). We use this direct physical measurement, combined with four cosmic-ray composition models, each divided into five mass groups, to calibrate the detector's absolute energy response in the range of 4 - 37 TeV. We quantify the fractional deviation between the calibrated and simulated energy scales by determining a best-fit scale shift parameter of $ε$ =-0.04 $\pm$ 0.03. This yields a 95% confidence interval of -9% to +0.2% for the systematic energy scale deviation. Complementing the simulation based on hadronic interaction model, this geomagnetic calibration provides a data-driven physical validation of the simulated WCDA energy response, effectively bounding systematic uncertainties and refining the overall energy scale.
2611.24261.comment: 13 pages, 13 Figures and 4 Tables are included in draft
2611.24261.title: Calibration of LHAASO-WCDA Energy Scale using Cosmic Ray Moon Shadow

2611.24325.abstract: Input convex neural networks provide a natural way to enforce convexity globally through architectural constraints. We study how this structure-preserving approximation framework extends to semiconvex, quasiconvex, and convex transformable functions. For $C^{1,1}$ convex functions on compact convex domains, we establish the sharp $W^{1,p}$ minimax rate $m^{-1/d}$ under max-affine approximation with $m$ affine pieces, and show that every max-affine function admits an exact bounded-width ICNN representation with complexity linear in $m$. The same $W^{1,p}$ approximation rate extends to semiconvex functions through quadratic lifting and to convex transformable functions through monotone composition. For general Lipschitz quasiconvex functions, we develop a quantitative finite-probe approximation theory based on monotone responses to affine projections and obtain a structure-preserving IqCNN with an $L^\infty$ approximation guarantee. We further show that these approximation results extend to ReLU-transferable smooth activations, including Softplus and ELU. Numerical experiments on PDE-based approximation problems compare the proposed architectures with parameter-matched MLPs and validation-tuned shape penalties, demonstrating global structural validity without penalty tuning while maintaining competitive approximation accuracy. Overall, the results identify recoverable convex latent structure as the key mechanism enabling gradient-level structure-preserving approximation beyond convexity.
2611.24325.title: Structure-Preserving Neural Approximation of Convex, Semiconvex, and Quasiconvex Functions

2611.24327.abstract: Embodied AI systems, such as drones and autonomous vehicles, improve navigation by enhancing perception in environments containing unseen objects. While Visual Language Models (VLMs) offer strong image understanding, their real-world application is underexplored. For effective deployment, open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) models, leveraging models like CLIP to assign pixel-level labels from text, must be robust to outdoor conditions, adverse weather, and varying viewpoints. Despite their potential, these models encounter significant challenges in cross-domain generalization, hindering their practical use in embodied AI applications. In this work, we present Pixel2Perspective, a benchmark for multi-angle object localization and open-vocabulary segmentation across both aerial and ground perspectives. This benchmark supports thorough evaluation across different viewpoints and sensor modalities. We assess foundational models like CLIP and advanced OVSS models using a curated dataset that spans varied outdoor conditions, sim-to-real scenarios, and multiple sensors, including infrared, to support the development of robust and generalizable perception systems. We also present a novel framework, Multi-Source RGB-IR Uncertainty Quantification (MSRIQ), which jointly models aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties across RGB and infrared imagery. This approach supports robust evaluation of open-vocabulary segmentation models across diverse environmental conditions. Our work sets a robustness-driven benchmark, providing key insights and laying the foundation for future research in open-world embodied AI perception. The benchmark and project page are available at https://aniruddhsikdar1.github.io/publications/pixel2perspective/
2611.24327.title: Pixel2Perspective: A Benchmark for Multi-Modal and Multi-View Generalization in Vision-Language Models

2611.24347.abstract: The search for better models, whether expressed as analytical equations or neural architectures, has increasingly shifted from manual design toward data-driven automation. While a multitude of algorithms exist, ranging from exhaustive search to AlphaEvolve, recent advances in general-purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex raise the question: could providing such systems with a "model discovery recipe" be enough to discover or improve models? We present automodel, an agent skill for general model discovery. With case studies in astrophysics, cardiovascular dynamics, precision agriculture, traffic flow, and vehicle tire dynamics, we show how commercial agents equipped with automodel can successfully identify novel and scientifically-relevant models. Our findings suggest that encoding model-discovery methodology as a portable agent skill can provide a simple, interactive, powerful and broadly applicable alternative to domain-specific automated discovery pipelines. The skill is available at: https://github.com/unlayer-ai/automodel.
2611.24347.title: automodel: A Skill for Agentic Model Discovery

2611.24355.abstract: Residual-based methods, including physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), physics-informed Kolmogorov--Arnold networks, and some physics-informed neural operator architectures, approximate PDE solutions by minimizing a discrete least-squares loss formed from the PDE and boundary residuals over a prescribed trial class. This structure is shared by classical least-squares Kansa collocation, whose kernel trial spaces admit an established convergence theory. For neural trial classes, approximation power alone does not ensure that discrete residuals control the continuous solution error. For linear elliptic Dirichlet problems, we extend the kernel-based collocation framework to neural trial classes through elliptic regularity, discrete stability, and consistency. Elliptic regularity supplies the PDE estimate relating solution error to continuous residuals. Discrete stability identifies admissible trial subclasses in which continuous residuals are controlled by a computable discrete loss. This step also quantifies the required number of collocation points. Furthermore, the stability analysis naturally demands a scale-dependent, physics-balanced boundary weight. For the constrained problem, consistency requires accurate comparison functions within the same admissible subclass, a requirement not supplied by neural approximation estimates alone. Specializing to multilayer perceptrons with tanh activations (tanh-MLPs), we construct admissible comparison networks and establish convergence for the constrained residual minimization problem. We further obtain conditional convergence of unconstrained physics-balanced PINNs based on tanh-MLPs under joint network and sampling refinement.
2611.24355.title: Stable admissible neural classes and convergent physics-informed neural networks

2611.24370.abstract: Stellar orbits around Sagittarius A*, in particular that of S2, test the spacetime of the Galactic Center. Such analyses usually integrate the equations of motion for every likelihood evaluation and sample the posterior.
